items.title: 61530_Roy Eldridge oral history interview
items.q: Boy, when I was with Horace Henderson, man, I used to get so mad when they'd play something slow.

ctx.x: So that's the way that works out, you know. I don't know... The Blues is something that was just... I didn't like ballads either then! And I think the reason I didn't like them was I couldn't play them. I'll be honest with you, you know. I hear a lot of cats now, they're playing ballads and they have to triple it up, you know. Playing in the meter is a little harder than being... You know, playing fast, all you got to do is spend a little time and rehearse, just rehearse, what are you going to riff, you're going…
When did you go with Horace? Was that after you came off the road with...?

items.title: 68514_Horace Henderson oral history interview
items.q: he was in my band for quite a few years. Then, of course, I would always tell my brother, you know, about anybody great like that. And when I rejoined my brother, I took Roy with me, and we got this Chicago job at the Grand Terrace -- Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry and joined John Fletcher

ctx.x: At the Grant Terrace. Uh-huh. Great.

I later joined Fletcher at the Grant Terrace when our band broke up. I joined Fletcher; I took Israel Crosby with me. I took Roy Eldridge with me, and Chu Berry was always there with Fletcher, and we had another tenor saxophonist. He was a great saxophonist. He just died recently -- named Elmer Williams. He had a beautiful tone. This was during the time that Coleman Hawkins decided to accept Jack Hilton's offer in Europe and go to Europe. So Fletcher

had to get a combination of the two -- Chu Berry, who could swing, but didn't have the tone And all that Hawk had, but Elmer Williams had the tone, so he had to get the combination of the two together so he could play his arrangement, because everything Fletcher had was built around Hawkins in his arrangement.
